title: Org-aware routing playbook for tenant tiering & noisy-neighbor controls
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for org/tenant-aware routing decisions in Redwood's control plane. Focus: how we classify tenants (tiering, contract SLAs), enforce quotas and fair-share, and protect latency-critical tenants from noisy neighbors across multi-region deployments.

Scope and required guarantees:
- Compatibility with hosted API, Dedicated, and Private control planes (same policy primitives).
- Strong SLOs for top-tier customers (p99 latency, availability) with automated fallback to compatible variants when needed.
- Predictable per-tenant cost accounting for billing and quota enforcement.
- Mitigation techniques for noisy neighbors with minimal impact on correctness.
- Routing decisions must be auditable and reversible (for postmortem and billing disputes).

Background/context notes (notes-to-self):
- Recent P0 incident: single mid-market tenant generated a burst that increased p99 by 3x for other tenants in the same pool. Root cause: lack of admission control + shared KV cache thrashing.
- We have three logical tiers today: free, standard, enterprise (and a small set of custom SLA tiers under contracts). How these map to routing priority is currently underspecified.

High-level architecture (control-plane interaction):
- Control plane components involved: Tenant Catalog (static metadata), SLA & Contract Store, Quota Engine, Policy Evaluator, Global Router (decision plane), Local Agent (region-level enforcer), Serving Pool Manager.
- Decision flow: incoming request -> authenticate -> enrich with tenant metadata -> policy evaluation (quota, tier, region affinity, contract flags) -> admission decision + route to pool/variant -> local agent applies throttles / cache-scoping.

Policy primitives we need (rough list):
- tier_priority (integer): higher wins for admission and preemption.
- hard_quota_tokens (rate or burst tokens): enforced at edge + region agent.
- fair_share_weight (float): for proportional allocation when overloaded.
- region_affinity (list): preferred regions per tenant (compliance/data residency).
- allow_burst_window (ms/minutes) and burst_budget (tokens): permit temporary bursts for high-tier customers.
- contract_fallback_model: explicit model name to fall back to when primary model is unavailable.
- noisiness_score_window: sliding-window metric to detect noisy neighbors (based on token/latency/error/queue length signal).

Routing decision flow (detailed steps):
1) Lookup tenant metadata and contracts in Tenant Catalog (must be cached in control plane for <100ms lookup).
2) Check region_affinity and data residency constraints; if mismatch -> route to nearest compliant region or reject with actionable error.
3) Consult Quota Engine: compute available tokens. If tokens exist -> continue. If exhausted -> see tier_priority and burst budget.
4) If under overload, run admission algorithm: 
   - Identify candidate pools (same model family, quantization/latency tradeoffs).
   - Score pools by: latency headroom, cost_tier, current_load, region_affinity.
   - Apply policy: preempt lower priority backlog if allowed (only for enterprise > standard; preemption limited to X% of capacity).
5) Emit route decision and attach enforcement instructions (throttle rate, KV-cache-scope id, model variant id).
6) Local agent enforces throttles and ensures per-tenant metrics are tagged.

Admission and fair-share algorithm (proposal):
- Normal mode (below 70% pool utilization): allocate based on requested tokens, respect burst budgets.
- Degraded mode (>= 70%): switch to weighted fair queueing using fair_share_weight. Enforce hard caps for free and standard tiers.
- Emergency mode (>= 95%): reserve X% capacity for enterprise+SLA tiers; remaining capacity split by weight. Optionally spin up burst capacity if autoscaler has resources.

Noisy neighbor controls (mechanisms):
- Admission throttling: tighten per-tenant rate limits dynamically using noisiness_score.
- Cache partitioning: tag KV cache entries with tenant id and evict by tenant; maintain min-reserved cache size for SLA tenants.
- Queue shaping & isolation: per-tenant request queues with bounded depth; backpressure to upstream clients (429 or retry-after headers).
- Preemption: selectively drop/slow lower-priority queued requests when higher-tier requests are pending, within contractual limits.
- Model variant degradation: switch noisy tenant to a lower-cost/fast model variant (with warning) when they breach throttles.
- Account-level circuit breaker: temporarily downgrade or suspend tenants who repeatedly exceed negotiated behavior; require human review for contract tiers.

Per-tenant cache strategy (notes):
- Global KV cache is the biggest source of cross-tenant interference. Plan: implement tenant-aware hash namespaces and soft reservations.
- Reservation policy: SLA tenants get N% of cache memory per pool; others share remaining with LRU eviction.
- Monitoring: per-tenant cache hit rate, eviction rate, and effective latency contribution.

SLA and contractual enforcement (billing ties):
- SLA violations must be recorded as auditable events (timestamped decision + metrics attached).
- When SLA is missed for enterprise customers, trigger automated credit calculation workflow linked to the request-level traces.
- For quota overruns, decision must include reason and yanked tokens count to support billing adjustments.

Multi-region considerations and routing heuristics:
- Primary mapping: tenant -> primary-region(s) (for latency) + allowed-failover regions.
- Cross-region failover: prefer local-region pools that meet tier/SLA; if not available, attempt nearest failover pool with compatible model variant.
- Sticky routing: use soft-affinity (cookie or request header-level affinity) to enhance cache/KV locality but allow control-plane to override on overload.
- Global pool vs region-local pools: prefer region-local unless enterprise contract explicitly states global pooled capacity.

Observability and telemetry requirements (must ship with policy):
- Tagging: every request must include tenant_id, tier, route_decision_id, pool_id, model_variant, and control-plane-policy-version.
- Metrics: per-tenant token_consumed, p50/p95/p99 latency, queue_depth, throttled_count, cache_hit_rate, noisy_score.
- Traces: decision time breakdown (lookup, policy_eval, scoring). Route decisions persisted for 90 days for audit.
- Alerts: automatic noisy-neighbor alert when noisiness_score > threshold for N minutes; escalate to ops when p99 for other tenants increases by >20%.

Compatibility matrix (short):
- Hosted API: full feature set.
- Dedicated: control-plane may be shared or dedicated per customer; when dedicated, allow simplified policy (no preemption of customer-qualified pools).
- Private: customers may opt out of global telemetry sharing; still require minimal event stream for billing/audit (encrypted).

Config examples (illustrative, not final):
- policy snippet (human-readable):
  tenant_id: acme-inc
  tier_priority: 90
  hard_quota_tokens: 10000/min
  fair_share_weight: 2.0
  region_affinity: [us-west-2, us-east-1]
  allow_burst_window: 120s
  burst_budget: 5000
  noisiness_score_window: 60s
  contract_fallback_model: redwood-fast-1b-quant

Operational rollout notes (proposal):
- Phase 0: gather telemetry and simulate decisions for 4 weeks (dry-run mode) with policy-evaluation tags on responses.
- Phase 1: enable soft enforcement (throttle warnings but do not deny), run for 2 weeks. Measure false positives.
- Phase 2: enable hard admission controls for free/standard tiers with enterprise preserved capacity.
- Phase 3: enable preemption and cross-tenant cache partitions.
- Phase 4: document SLAs and make UI toggles in console for per-tenant overrides.

Open questions / tradeoffs to decide (for next design meeting):
- Preemption policy: what fraction of capacity is safe to preempt without violating contracts on the lower-priority side? (Proposal: cap preemption to 10% of pool capacity, configurable per-pool.)
- Cache reservation granularity: per-pool vs per-host. Do we suffer cold-starts when shifting tenants across hosts?
- Billing/credits automation: what is the exact data to persist for accurate automated crediting? (Request-level traces vs aggregated windows).
- How aggressive should automatic model-variant fallback be for enterprise customers? Should we require a pre-approved list in contract?

Action items and owners (next 6 weeks):
- Build detection prototype for noisiness_score in serving runtime (owner: Sanjay Kapoor) - due 2026-03-01.
- Implement control-plane tenant lookup cache with TTL and fallbacks (owner: Elena Park) - due 2026-02-28.
- Simulate admission control algorithms on historical traffic (owner: James O'Neill) - due 2026-02-20.
- Draft console UI changes for per-tenant overrides and SLA view (owner: Maya Lopez) - due 2026-03-15.

Notes to reviewers: this is a working doc; expect iterations. We need to validate the proposed thresholds with SRE and Product (pricing implications). If you have customer contract edge cases, paste them into the linked Confluence page.
